Bondman
BOND-man
noun
From bond (that which binds) and man; a man bound to service. In the Authorized Version it renders the Hebrew 'ebed, a servant, most often one who has sold himself for debt.

Biblical Definition

A bondman is a man bound to service. The Authorized Version uses the word chiefly for the Hebrew who, sinking into poverty, sold his labour to a brother until the debt was worked off. The Mosaic code hedges that condition about on every side. He is not to be treated as a chattel: “if thy brother that dwelleth by thee be waxen poor, and be sold unto thee; thou shalt not compel him to serve as a bondservant” (Lev 25:39) — he is to be as a hired servant, not ruled over with rigour (Lev 25:43). His term is fixed: “if thy brother, an Hebrew man, or an Hebrew woman, be sold unto thee, and serve thee six years; then in the seventh year thou shalt let him go free from thee” (Deu 15:12), and not empty-handed, but furnished liberally from flock, floor, and winepress. The reason given is redemption remembered: “thou shalt remember that thou wast a bondman in the land of Egypt, and the LORD thy God redeemed thee” (Deu 15:15). And there is one more provision, the loveliest in the code. If the servant will not go out because he loves his master and his master’s house, his ear is bored through with an aul at the door and he serves for ever (Deu 15:16–17). The bondslave by love, not by debt — and in Psa 40:6 the Messiah says, mine ears hast thou opened.

Webster 1828 Definition

A man bound to service; in the Mosaic law, a Hebrew sold for debt, protected by statute and released in the seventh year.

BONDMAN, a man in bondage; a servant bound to service without wages, as opposed to a freeman.

From bond, that which binds, and man; rendering the Hebrew 'ebed.

The Hebrew bondman served six years and went free in the seventh (Deu 15:12).

He might not be ruled over with rigour, nor sold as a bondman (Lev 25:42-43).

Manstealing, the seizing and selling of a man, was a capital crime (Exo 21:16).

Key Scripture

Lev 25:39 — "And if thy brother that dwelleth by thee be waxen poor, and be sold unto thee; thou shalt not compel him to serve as a bondservant:"

Deu 15:12 — "And if thy brother, an Hebrew man, or an Hebrew woman, be sold unto thee, and serve thee six years; then in the seventh year thou shalt let him go free from thee."

Deu 15:15 — "And thou shalt remember that thou wast a bondman in the land of Egypt, and the LORD thy God redeemed thee: therefore I command thee this thing to day."

Exo 21:16 — "And he that stealeth a man, and selleth him, or if he be found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death."

Modern Corruption

The charge that Scripture endorses chattel slavery collapses on the text: the law it actually gives makes manstealing a capital crime and sets the bondman free with a full hand.

expand to see more

The accusation is made constantly and it must be answered plainly, not hedged. Scripture does not endorse chattel slavery; it prescribes the death penalty for the trade that creates it. “He that stealeth a man, and selleth him, or if he be found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death” (Exo 21:16), and Paul lists menstealers with murderers and perjurers as contrary to sound doctrine (1Ti 1:10). Every man in the African slave trade — the raider, the shipper, the auctioneer, the buyer holding stolen men — stood under a capital sentence from the law he claimed to honour. The Mosaic institution is a different thing entirely: an indenture entered by a man’s own act to discharge a debt, with a fixed six-year term, release in the seventh, release at Jubilee, a liberal severance out of the master’s own goods, a prohibition of rigour, freedom for any servant maimed by his master, and a standing refusal to return a fugitive (Deu 23:15–16) — the exact reverse of the fugitive-slave laws that disgraced the Christian West. The wickedness of race-based chattel slavery is not softened by biblical precedent; it is condemned by biblical law, and by the abolitionists who read that law rightly.

The doctrine to recover from this word is the aul in the ear. The law provided a way out for the man who did not want one: “if he say unto thee, I will not go away from thee; because he loveth thee and thine house, because he is well with thee” (Deu 15:16), then his ear was bored through at the door and he served for ever — a freeman who chose bondage out of love. The Psalmist puts that language in the mouth of the Messiah: “Sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire; mine ears hast thou opened… I delight to do thy will, O my God” (Psa 40:6, 8), and Hebrews reads it of Christ coming into the world: “a body hast thou prepared me… Lo, I come… to do thy will, O God” (Heb 10:5, 7). He was under no debt, no compulsion, no necessity. He took upon Him the form of a servant (Php 2:7) because He loved the Father and loved the house, and He wears the marks of that willing bondage in His hands for ever. Every ransomed sinner is thereby made the Lord’s freeman — and, in the same breath, Christ’s servant (1Co 7:22).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

A man bound to service; in Israel a debtor with a fixed term, in Christ a servant by love.

expand to see more

Bondman — bond, that which binds, + man.

Hebrew 'ebed, servant; Greek doulos, bondservant.

Six years' service, freedom in the seventh, and a liberal parting gift (Deu 15:12-14).

Manstealing was capital under Moses and is condemned by Paul (Exo 21:16; 1Ti 1:10).

The aul through the ear marked the servant who would not go free (Deu 15:17).

Usage

"Remember that thou wast a bondman in Egypt: redemption remembered makes a merciful master."

"The law that regulated the bondman hanged the manstealer — Exo 21:16 ends the argument."

"The aul in the ear: a servant who stays because he loves his master — and so did Christ."
